title: Call No Man Happy
notes: Point of view: narration is Solon in the first person (the card's speaker) on every panel except p3.4, the coda, which is Glauka (narr_voice: glauka). The lettered captions stay third person ('Then Solon travelled').
p1.1: the 'LEGEND?' tag sits on Solon's reforms, which are history. Narrated over; the card flags page 1 history. Optional patch: change tag to HISTORY.
p1.1: the Parthenon is drawn on the Acropolis behind Solon, about 150 years too early. Narration does not mention it. Low priority.
p3.4: Glauka's sign reads 'GLAUKA' and the lettered bubble says 'LEGEND?'. The script's 'speech' is null although a bubble is lettered; left unchanged as instructed. Patch the sign (audit 6.3).
Scene: the Pnyx assembly place post-dates Solon; the scene says only 'From this hill you can see the whole city', which is true and does not place Solon's lawgiving on the Pnyx.
p3.3: narration is under 12 words on purpose (climax: the lettered 'Solon! Solon! Solon!' does the work).

panels.visual: Solon (wise old man, wide hat, staff, white beard) on the Pnyx hill speaking to a crowd of Athenian citizens, hand raised, golden light
panels.caption: Around 594 BC, Athens chose Solon to fix its laws.
panels.narr: I have been everywhere, children, and I will tell you all of it. But first: around 594 BC Athens was in a mess, so it chose me, Solon, to fix its laws.

panels.visual: Solon tearing up a scroll of old laws, chains of debtors falling off several Athenians who rejoice
panels.caption: He cancelled most of the old laws and freed Athenians sold as slaves for debt.
panels.narr: Poor Athenians who could not pay their debts were being sold as slaves. I cancelled most of the old laws and set them free. Chains are heavy. Laws should be lighter.

panels.visual: An ancient court and a thief with a single cabbage, a stern judge shouting 'Death!', comic horror
panels.caption: The laws of Draco were so harsh that stealing a cabbage could be punished with death.
panels.narr: Before me, Athens used the laws of Draco. They were so harsh that stealing a cabbage could get you killed. A cabbage! I have met many cabbages. None was worth a man.

panels.visual: A scroll of Draco's laws dripping red ink drawn as 'written in blood', comic, no gore
panels.caption: People said they were written in blood.
panels.narr: People said Draco's laws were written in blood, not ink. Even today you call a cruel rule draconian. Mine were kinder. Kind laws last longer than cruel ones.

panels.visual: Solon travelling on foot along a road with a staff and a travel bag, eagle in the sky
panels.caption: Then Solon travelled.
panels.narr: Then I travelled. I left Athens for ten years, so nobody could make me change my laws. A wise man does not stay home to argue with his own rules.

panels.visual: A glittering hall of treasure: heaps of gold and gems; Croesus, king of Lydia (plump, jewelled, proud) showing off to Solon
panels.caption: Herodotus says he visited Croesus, the richest man in the world.

speech.speaker: Croesus
speech.text: Who is the happiest man alive?

panels.narr: Herodotus says I visited Croesus, king of Lydia, the richest man in the world. His servants showed me every room of his treasure. Then the king asked his question.

voice_speech.speaker: Croesus
voice_speech.text: Tell me, Athenian: who is the happiest man alive?

panels.visual: Croesus leaning forward expecting to hear his own name, big hopeful grin
panels.caption: He expected Solon to say him.
panels.narr: He expected me to say him. Look at that face. A man who asks that question with gold all round him does not want an answer. He wants a mirror.

panels.visual: Solon calmly shaking his head and pointing at a simple Athenian soldier in a distant battle
panels.caption: Solon named an ordinary Athenian who died bravely in battle.

speech.speaker: Solon
speech.text: Call no man happy until he is dead.

panels.narr: I named Tellus, an ordinary Athenian. He had fine sons, saw their children born, and died bravely in battle for his city. Croesus was furious. I told him why.

panels.visual: King Cyrus of Persia and his army overrunning the golden city of Sardis, flames and banners
panels.caption: Years later Croesus lost his kingdom to the Persian king Cyrus.
panels.narr: Years later Croesus lost his kingdom to the Persian king Cyrus. His city, his gold, his throne: all of it gone in one war.

panels.visual: Croesus bound on a high burning pyre, bursting flames, Cyrus watching
panels.caption: He was put on a burning pyre.
panels.narr: Cyrus had him tied up on a great pyre of wood and set it alight. The richest man in the world. All he had left was one sentence.

panels.visual: Croesus' face in a halo of flames shouting a name, desperate
panels.caption: He cried out Solon's name three times.
panels.narr: In the flames, he remembered me.

panels.visual: A sudden rainstorm falling from the sky over the pyre, Cyrus looking up in wonder; in a corner Glauka the owl holds up a tiny wooden sign on which is lettered exactly the word LEGEND? (a question mark after it; the sign does not say Glauka)
panels.caption: A sudden rainstorm put the fire out. But Croesus and Solon may never have met.
panels.narr: Only Apollo's rain could put the fire out. That's a legend: a real person, and a story that grew around him. Croesus became king when Solon was very old. They may never have met.
